title: Graph: the market for ideas
scenario: The market for ideas: the fragmentation index on the vertical axis (Europe high, China low) and the number of ideas on the horizontal. Two curves: size of audience and risk of persecution.

questions.stem: Which curve is the supply side of the market for ideas?
questions.explanation: Higher fragmentation lowers persecution risk, so more ideas are supplied: upward slope.

questions.stem: Where is China on the graph?
choices: Top right: high fragmentation, many ideas
Bottom left: low fragmentation, few ideas
Top left: high fragmentation, few ideas
Bottom right: low fragmentation, many ideas
questions.explanation: Unified China has the lowest fragmentation index and ends up with a low number of ideas.

questions.stem: Africa sits high on the fragmentation index but far to the left on ideas. What explains this?
choices: A very large audience in each state
A lack of intellectual consolidation and low payoffs relative to the cost of ideas
questions.explanation: Fragmentation is not sufficient on its own.

questions.stem: At Europe's level of fragmentation, the persecution curve reaches E₁ (many ideas) but the audience curve only E'' (few). What lifted Europe toward many ideas?
choices: The Republic of Letters: a unified market for ideas across fragmented states
questions.explanation: Fragmentation kept persecution low, and the transnational Republic of Letters removed the small-audience problem. Together with lower access costs and an urban commercial class, Europe moved to greater levels of ideas.

questions.stem: Because fragmentation shifts both demand and supply of ideas, the model has multiple equilibria.
questions.explanation: The two channels pull in opposite directions, so different fragmentation levels give different outcomes (China, Europe, Africa).
